facts.fact: Name for the term: "Tannin"
Name for the term: "tannin"
Name for the term: "tanin"
Tannins are natural compounds that leaves, seed pods and wood release as they break down in water.
Tannins from wood are mainly humic and fulvic acids.
Every kind of wood releases tannin when soaked in water.
Tannins tint water golden to brown, like black tea.
A little tannin makes water slightly yellow; more turns it tea-coloured or brown.
Tannin does not make water cloudy; haze points to other causes such as bacterial blooms or suspended debris.
Tannins lower pH and soften the water.
Leaves and peat lower pH only slightly and gradually, not drastically and quickly.
Tannin is a weak acid, and how far it moves pH depends on KH.
In hard water with high alkalinity, the pH-lowering effect of tannin sources is quite fleeting.
The page says that with tap-water KH of 3 to 6, tannin shifts pH by less than 0.2, while in RO water with KH near 0 a pH crash is possible.
Tannins are described as usually harmless and not toxic to fish, plants or invertebrates.
Tannin does not directly harm fish but can drop pH sharply and stress them.
By cutting light penetration and lowering pH, tannins may limit algae growth.
AquaScape says tannin does not kill algae directly; it only slows light-dependent algae by reducing light.
AquaScape says tannin may inhibit some microbes but is not a medicine and cannot replace disease treatment.
Fish from blackwater habitats, such as tetras, bettas and dwarf cichlids, benefit most from tannin-stained water.
Leaf tannins give a brownish tinge suited to fish from dark, soft Amazonian waters; Uaru use lignite as an egg-laying substrate.
Too much tannin can make fish mucus coagulate and clog the gill filaments; a fish gasping at the surface may be suffering from this.
Excess tannins can also irritate fish skin.
For a tannin overdose, do an immediate, large water change and remove loose leaves or peat fibres.
Adding many leaves or cones at once can cause a sudden acid spike.
Adding tannin sources to hard-water tanks of Malawi and Tanganyika cichlids, which need hard, alkaline water.
With tap water KH below 3-4 dKH, tannins can push pH down faster than expected.
In hard water above 10 dGH, tannins will not overcome the buffering for a blackwater tank.
Skipping the pre-soak can lead to months of brown water.
Pine and other softwoods leak resin, and wood from roadsides or sprayed land should not be used.
Fresh wood should not be used straight away, as some wood such as pine can contain toxic resin.
Wood that is soft or rotting should not be used; test it by pressing with a fingernail.
AquaScape says boiling never removes all tannin.
Aquasetup says boiling removes only the tannin in the outer layer, so the inside keeps leaching for one or more months.
Driftwood releases most of its tannin in the first 2 to 3 months, then far less, and almost never stops completely.
Most wood slows its tannin release significantly within 4-12 weeks; a small pre-soaked piece may stop tinting within 2-4 weeks.
Activated carbon can clear tannin-tinted water within 24-48 hours and typically saturates after 3-4 weeks.
Remove activated carbon before medicating, because it also removes medications.
Activated carbon can improve clarity within a few hours and is exhausted in 2-4 weeks.
Seachem Purigen can remove tannins, odours and organic wastes quickly.
For heavy tinting, do 25-30% water changes two or three times a week for the first month.
For yellow water, do about 30% water changes every 2-3 days in the first weeks, or use activated carbon or Purigen in the filter.
For yellow water, do 30% water changes 2-3 times a week and put a bag of activated carbon in the filter.
Water changes only dilute tannin and are not a permanent fix.
Scrub dirt and soft bark off the wood under running water.
Scrub the wood with a stiff brush, without soap.
Boil the wood for 1-2 hours to kill microbes and draw out tannin; the boil water turns dark brown.
A rolling boil for 1-2 hours drives out many tannins and helps sterilise the wood; large pieces can be done in sections.
After boiling, soak the wood for a few more days before it goes in the tank.
Soak the wood in clean water for a few days to a few weeks, changing the water daily until it stays only slightly yellow.
Change soak water daily or every two days; once it stays mostly clear after 24-48 hours, most free tannins are gone.
Soak driftwood in a separate tank for a few weeks to a few months, with regular water changes.
For natural wood you collect yourself, dry it in strong sun for about 2 months or more, knock off soil, brush it and sand off leftover bark.
Soak the wood for a few days to one or two weeks so it releases tannin, absorbs water and sinks more easily.
Large pieces that cannot be boiled can have hot water poured over them section by section.
Wood can be baked at no more than 121°C.
Another method: soak in salt solution for 1 week, then in water for 2 to 3 weeks.
Aquasetup advises against boiling driftwood, saying it damages the inner structure and makes the wood rot faster.
A white slime often appears on new wood a few days after it goes in; it is common, does not harm the tank and can be food for fish or shrimp.
The white or cloudy film on new wood is biofilm, not harmful mould, and usually fades in 1–2 weeks.
White mould on driftwood can be brushed off or left, as it may disappear on its own.
Most driftwood floats at first because it dried out in the forest or in transport; it sinks only once fully saturated.
Floating wood can be weighted with stones, or have weights screwed on and hidden under plants such as Anubias.
In Vietnam, dried Indian almond leaves ("Lá Bàng Khô") are the most common tannin source, cheap and widely used, especially by betta breeders.
"Lũa Tự Nhiên (Driftwood)" is listed as a tannin source alongside "Lá Bàng Khô (Indian Almond Leaves)", "Lá Sồi (Oak Leaves)", "Alder Cone (Quả Cây Trăn Châu Âu)" and "Than Bùn (Peat Moss)".
"Lũa Sa Tùng (Cholla Wood)": tube-shaped with many holes, a good hiding place for shrimp.
"Lũa Sa Tùng" (also called "lũa xương chùm"): medium sinking, releases a lot of tannin, dark brown wood.
"Lũa Đỗ Quyên": harder to sink, releases little to medium tannin, light yellowish-brown wood.
"Lũa Đỗ Quyên": curved, soft-looking branches for natural layouts.
"Lũa đỗ quyên": many softly curved branches, brighter yellow than other kinds, turns deep brown when soaked.
"Lũa Linh Sam": sinks fast, releases medium tannin, reddish-brown wood.
"Lũa Linh Sam": very common, varied shapes, durable in water.
"Lũa linh sam": comes in many sizes with grain patterns, from straight to curved.
"Lũa bonsai/ lũa xương chùm": root and trunk pieces shaped like bonsai, containing a fairly large amount of tannin.
"Lũa bonsai/ lũa xương chùm" has sharp edges unsuitable for long-finned fish such as bettas and guppies.
"Lũa cholla": dried cactus wood from desert regions of Arizona and New Mexico, cylindrical, hollow and full of small holes; it releases tannin.
"Lũa săn đá": medium to large, mostly hollow pieces with many grain streaks, left when a big trunk erodes.
"Lũa rễ rừng": small, long, soft root pieces in clusters, also used in blackwater biotope aquascapes.
"Lũa hải sơn quỳ": sold as a whole trunk with roots, mostly straight, suited to pillar-style layouts.
"Lũa thạch sùng": straight processed wood that keeps its bark, often paired with root wood for forest layouts.
"Lũa Hải Sơn Tùng": many small branches, suited to forest-style layouts.
"Gỗ lũa Linh Sam" is commonly used in planted tanks, while dead mangrove stumps ("gốc chết của sú, vẹt, đước") are less durable and less attractive.
Mopani and Malaysian driftwood release heavy tannins, while spider wood and cholla release far less; bogwood is among the most tannin-rich.
Large mopani can keep releasing tannins for 2-3 months and may need 3-4 weeks of soaking.
